findings.claim: Whole-novel question ends “You must refer to the context of the novel in your answer.”

findings.claim: “When the narrator describes Mr Collins as believing he has ‘every possible right’ to Elizabeth’s hand”
findings.truth: “every possible right” does not appear anywhere in the novel. The narrator’s actual phrase for Collins after the refusal is “wilful self-deception”.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1342 ch. 19: “To such perseverance in wilful self-deception Elizabeth would make no reply”; no match for “every possible right” in the full text

findings.claim: “How despicably I have acted!”
findings.truth: Austen writes “How despicably have I acted!” — verb before subject.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1342 ch. 36: “‘How despicably have I acted!’ she cried. ‘I, who have prided myself on my discernment!’”

findings.claim: Flashcard answer quotes “How despicably I have acted!”
findings.truth: Same word-order error on the memorisation card.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1342 ch. 36

findings.claim: “Wickham squandered the church living, demanded £3,000 instead”
findings.truth: The order is reversed. Wickham resigned his claim to the living, took £3,000 in exchange, spent it, and only then asked for the living back.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1342 ch. 35 (Darcy’s letter): “resigning all claim to assistance in the church ... and accepted in return three thousand pounds”

findings.claim: Georgiana is “the opposite of the proud, haughty sister Miss Bingley’s gossip suggested”
findings.truth: It is Wickham who calls Georgiana “very, very proud”. Miss Bingley praises Georgiana’s beauty and accomplishments.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1342 ch. 16 (Wickham): “she is too much like her brother,--very, very proud”; Miss Bingley’s letter: “I really do not think Georgiana Darcy has her equal for beauty, elegance, and accomplishments”

findings.claim: Key Fact quotes Mrs Reynolds as “I have never known a cross word from him”
findings.truth: Mrs Reynolds says “I have never had a cross word from him in my life”.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1342 ch. 43

findings.claim: “Elizabeth receives the news at the Pemberley inn”
findings.truth: There is no inn at Pemberley. Elizabeth and the Gardiners are staying at the inn in Lambton when Jane’s letters arrive.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1342 ch. 46, set at Lambton

findings.claim: Flashcard asks “Which Darcy line at Pemberley admits love grew beyond his control?”
findings.truth: “I was in the middle before I knew that I had begun” is spoken at Longbourn in ch. 60, after the engagement. The card contradicted its own lesson body, which already carries that correction.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1342 ch. 60; lesson body: “(Chapter 60, spoken after the engagement — not during the Pemberley episode)”

findings.claim: Lady Catherine’s visit backfiring is labelled “dramatic irony”, defined as “a situation in which an action intended to produce one outcome actually produces the opposite result”
findings.truth: That is situational irony. Dramatic irony is the audience knowing something a character does not. The glossary entry and the L8 quotation bank carried the same mislabel.
findings.evidence: standard AO2 terminology; the definition in data-def is the definition of situational irony

findings.claim: Model answer quotes “selfish disdain for the feelings of others”
findings.truth: Elizabeth says “selfish disdain of the feelings of others”.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1342 ch. 34

findings.claim: Wickham “elopes with fifteen-year-old Lydia”
findings.truth: Lydia is sixteen at the elopement. Georgiana was the fifteen-year-old.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1342 ch. 49 (Mrs Bennet): “she was only sixteen last June”, and the elopement is that August; ch. 35: Georgiana “was then but fifteen”

findings.claim: Sixteen whole-novel questions (index 1 and index 4 in every lesson) are typed “20 marks — Extract Analysis”
findings.truth: These are part (b) whole-text essays, not part (a) extract questions. Relabelled “20 marks — Part (b) Whole-Text Essay”.
findings.evidence: spec: Section A part 1 is the printed extract of about 400 words; part 2 explores the whole text

findings.claim: Every mark scheme in the unit labels two different bands “Top band” (17-20 and 13-16) and names the bottom band “Lower band”. The 4-mark schemes use “Upper band” and “Lower band”.
findings.truth: The house ladder is Top band / Upper-mid band / Mid band / Lower-mid band / Low band / Basic band. Option (a): leave the 48 schemes to the programme’s queued band-ladder sweep, which can relabel them consistently across subjects. Option (b): relabel here as 17-20 Top band, 13-16 Upper-mid band, 9-12 Mid band, 5-8 Lower-mid band, 1-4 Low band. Recommend (a) — the fault is uniform and mechanical, and one sweep avoids two different ladders landing in the same subject.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT house ladder; 48 practice questions in this unit

findings.claim: Sixteen questions are typed “4 marks — Quote Analysis”
findings.truth: This board sets no 4-mark question on the 19th-century novel; both parts are 20 marks. The items are useful quotation drills, so the honest label is a revision task rather than an exam question, but that is a house-format decision rather than a fact fix.
findings.evidence: spec raw-mark table: Component 2 Section A is 20 + 20

findings.claim: The L3, L5 and L6 exam tips coach part (b) as a methods-and-structure essay (“use the letter as a structural pivot”, “the examiner rewards structural awareness”, “explain how the language reveals character”).
findings.truth: Part (b) is marked for AO1 only, so methods analysis earns nothing there. The L8 instances are fixed in this pass. Option (a): reword each tip so the method advice points at part (a) and part (b) becomes argument and evidence. Option (b): leave them, on the view that a critical style naturally references method. Recommend (a) — it is the same error as F22 and each is a one-sentence edit, but it touches three further narration blocks, so it is worth a nod first.
findings.evidence: spec raw-mark table: Component 2 questions 1b-7b = AO1 20

findings.claim: “My good opinion once lost, is lost forever.”
findings.truth: Austen has “My good opinion once lost is lost for ever” — no comma, and “for ever” as two words. The form used here is the standard popular rendering and appears five times across the lesson, so it is recorded rather than edited.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1342 ch. 11

summary: Eight lessons checked against Project Gutenberg #1342 and the Edexcel 1ET0 spec. Eleven HIGH findings: a fabricated Collins quotation, the “How despicably have I acted!” word order in four places, Mrs Reynolds’s “cross word” misquote, Georgiana’s pride attributed to Miss Bingley instead of Wickham, Lydia aged fifteen instead of sixteen, an AQA-style context rubric on a section where AO3 is not assessed, and an exam-technique panel giving both parts AO1 + AO2 when part (a) is AO2 only and part (b) AO1 only. Nine banned paper or band codes removed. Sixteen whole-novel questions were typed as extract analysis.
